## Quiz time {#dd-quiz}

**Raise your hand if you have already used:**

::: {.incremental}
- **VHDL**

- **Verilog or SystemVerilog**

- an **FPGA**

- an **ASIC design flow**
:::

::: {.fragment}
We will use short **SystemVerilog** examples. The concepts are independent of
the HDL syntax.
:::

## Combinational logic: which line runs first? {#dd-combinational}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```systemverilog
module mul_add4(
  input  logic [3:0] a, b, c,
  output logic [8:0] d
);
  logic [7:0] product;

  assign d =
      {1'b0, product} + {5'b0, c};

  assign product =
      {4'b0, a} * {4'b0, b};
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

The assignment to `d` is written first. Does the **adder** execute before the
**multiplier**?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Answer: neither line runs first.**

- The multiplier and adder are active concurrently.
- The adder settles after `product`, but it is not scheduled after it.
- With no register, there is no stored state or clock cycle.
:::
:::
::::

## Bit widths: where does the carry go? {#dd-widths}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```systemverilog
logic [3:0] a, b;
logic [3:0] wrapped;
logic [4:0] exact;

assign wrapped = a + b;
assign exact =
    {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b};
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

For `a = 15` and `b = 1`, what values reach `wrapped` and `exact`?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```text
wrapped = 4'b0000   // 0
exact   = 5'b10000  // 16
```

The extra carry exists only when the operands and result have room for it.
**Width is part of the hardware behavior.**
:::
:::
::::

## Registers: when does `q` change? {#dd-registers}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  q <= d;
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

If `d` changes between two rising clock edges, when can `q` change?
:::
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/register-timing.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="0" fig-alt="Timing diagram in which d changes between clock edges and q takes each new value only on the following rising edge" width="100%"}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
**Answer:** at the next rising edge. Between edges, `q` keeps its previous value.
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
A register introduces **state** and a **cycle boundary**. Combinational logic
still propagates between registers.
:::
:::
::::

## Hierarchy: how many datapaths exist? {#dd-hierarchy}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
```systemverilog
module pair(
  input  logic [3:0] a, b, c,
  output logic [8:0] d0, d1
);
  mul_add4 u_left(
    .a(a), .b(b), .c(c), .d(d0));

  mul_add4 u_right(
    .a(a), .b(c), .c(b), .d(d1));
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Does `pair` call `mul_add4` twice, or create **two datapaths**?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Answer: two datapaths:** two multipliers and two adders.

- A `module` defines a reusable boundary.
- Each instance creates hardware.
- Ports connect signals between instances.
- A hierarchy boundary adds no clock cycle.
:::
:::
::::

## FPGA: what must be configurable? {#dd-fpga-analogy}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="59%"}
![Left: a cellular automaton. Right: a simple FPGA. Adapted from [@popoff2026frugality].](assets/images/digital-design/fpga-cellular-automaton.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="A cellular automaton grid beside a simple FPGA grid with configurable cells and richer programmable interconnect" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="41%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

If one chip can become many circuits, which parts must be configurable?
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Logic:** LUT truth tables

- **State:** registers

- **Connections:** routing switches

- **Device:** manufactured once, configured for many circuits
:::
:::
::::

## FPGA: program or configured circuit? {#dd-fpga-configuration}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Left: a configurable logic cell containing a LUT and register. Right: one configured path through an FPGA. Adapted from [@popoff2026frugality].](assets/images/digital-design/fpga-lut-configured.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="A lookup-table cell with a one-bit register beside an FPGA fabric whose selected cells and routes are highlighted" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Is the bitstream executed one instruction at a time?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**No. It configures structure.**

- Place and route choose cells and connections.
- A 4-input LUT stores $2^4=16$ truth-table bits.
- The bitstream sets LUTs, registers, and routing switches.
:::

::: {.fragment}
During execution, connections stay fixed: signals propagate through
combinational paths and registers sample on clock edges.
:::
:::
::::

## FPGA: LUTs or a DSP block? {#dd-fpga-resources}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="36%"}
```systemverilog
assign product = a * b;
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Where can this multiplier be built?
:::
:::

::: {.column width="64%"}
::: {.fragment}
| FPGA resource | Hardware role |
|---|---|
| LUT + register | Boolean logic and state |
| routing | wires between resources |
| DSP block | hard multiplier or MAC |
| block RAM | on-chip storage |
:::

::: {.fragment}
The multiplier may use LUT logic or a hard DSP block. The target and synthesis
flow choose the resource; the arithmetic meaning stays the same
[@popoff2026frugality].
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
Modern devices also integrate I/O and, on some families, a CPU system.
:::

## ASIC: what becomes fixed? {#dd-asic-cells}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Which parts of this OR gate can be reconfigured after fabrication?
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="31%"}
**RTL**

```systemverilog
assign y = a | b;
```
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
![Logic schematic of a SKY130 OR2 standard cell. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/sky130-or2-schematic.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Schematic representation of a two-input OR standard cell" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
![Physical layout of the same SKY130 OR2 cell. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/sky130-or2-layout-cropped.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Colored GDSII geometry for a two-input OR standard cell" height="350"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
**Answer: none.** Logic synthesis chooses cells; place and route assigns their
coordinates and wires; fabrication fixes the geometry.
:::

## Physical design: what determines cost? {#dd-asic-layout}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![Placed-and-routed floating-point divider. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/gds-divider.jpg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Physical-design view of a routed floating-point divider with standard cells, clock tree, power grid, and signal wires" height="560"}
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Must two logically equivalent layouts have the same delay and area?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**No.** Physical cost depends on:

- Cells occupy **area**.

- Wires have **length, delay, and congestion**.

- Clock and power need their own networks.
:::
:::
::::

## Keep the questions explicit {#dd-vocabulary}

| Question from the example | Hardware concept | Compiler boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Which line runs first? | combinational dataflow | `comb` |
| Where does the carry go? | bit-vector width | `comb` types |
| When does `q` change? | register and clock | `seq` |
| How many datapaths exist? | module and instance | `hw` |
| Program or configured circuit? | LUT and DSP mapping | synthesis target |
| What becomes fixed? | cells, wires, floorplan | implementation |

::: {.fragment}
CIRCT keeps the first four distinctions explicit in `hw`, `comb`, and `seq`.
Later passes choose target resources and physical implementation.
:::
